KIRA R&D internship, 2026

HCl-resistant humidifier-dehumidifier prototype

As the sole R&D intern at KIRA, an MIT-founded water-treatment startup in Boston, I designed, built, and automated a lab-scale humidification-dehumidification (HDH) system that had to handle hot hydrochloric acid, run unattended, and keep going seven or more hours a day for a month.

Where
KIRA, Boston
When
June to August 2026
Role
R&D Engineering Intern, Controls & Hardware
Controls
CLICK PLC, Node-RED
Results
Redesigned the fluid routing to boost output 4×. Built PLC-based automated testing that cut test time by more than 65%.

Design process. Select a step to jump to it.

Requirements

Temperature
Up to 60 °C
Chemistry
Every wetted part resists highly corrosive hydrochloric acid
Controls
Runs autonomously
Duty cycle
7+ hours a day for at least one month
Cost
Parts available online or in the lab, or designed myself

Design

Materials

Key decision

Keep all metal out of the flow path

Hot hydrochloric acid corrodes most metals, and the system had to run seven or more hours a day for a month. We built it from acid-resistant plastics, and I redesigned the system so no metal remained inside the instruments the fluid passes through.

Printed parts
ABS, chosen for its resistance to HCl
Piping
CPVC, along with the purchased plastic parts
Instruments
Redesigned to remove all internal metal from the flow meters, valves, and sensors

Why the redesign was necessary

Hydrochloric acid attacks most common metals, including steel, aluminum, brass, and zinc, and heat speeds the reaction up. Even stainless steel isn’t safe: chloride ions break down the thin oxide layer that normally protects it, which leads to pitting. Leaving metal in the flow path would have caused four problems over a month of daily runs.

  • Leaks and part failureFittings, valve seats, and seals would corrode until they leaked or failed, long before the system finished its month-long run.
  • Bad sensor data, bad controlThe thin metal parts inside flow meters, valves, and sensors, like springs, shafts, and probes, have the least material to lose, so they fail first. A corroding sensor drifts, and because the CLICK PLC runs the system from those readings, bad data means bad control decisions.
  • Contaminated water and resultsCorroding metal dissolves into the water as metal ions. In a water-treatment prototype, that contaminates the product and makes results inconsistent from one test to the next.
  • Gas and pressureAcid reacting with metal releases hydrogen gas, which adds pressure inside a closed system.
Why ABS and CPVC
CPVC piping
Resists HCl and is rated to about 93 °C, well above the 60 °C operating temperature. Standard PVC tops out at 60 °C, and at that temperature keeps only about a fifth of its room-temperature pressure rating.
ABS printed parts
The custom parts had to be 3D printed. ABS resists dilute HCl and stays rigid well above 60 °C, while PLA, the most common printing plastic, softens at around 60 °C.
Why not acid-proof metals?
Metals that do survive hot HCl, like tantalum or nickel alloys such as Hastelloy, are expensive and hard to source. That conflicted with the requirement to use low-cost, readily available parts.

Built prototype

  • Runs autonomously on a CLICK PLC, using capacitive level sensors plus pressure, temperature, humidity, and weight readings as feedback to hold steady-state evaporation and condensation.
  • Every material in the system is rated for high temperature and HCl.
  • Comes apart quickly so sieves and filters can be swapped between tests.
  • Safety gauges keep pressure below a safe limit.

Lemelson-MIT InvenTeam, 2022–23

HippoBag, a smart backpack that notices what’s missing

With my high school’s Lemelson-MIT InvenTeam, I helped build a backpack that weighs its own contents and buzzes when something is left behind. I’m a co-inventor on the U.S. patent it earned, granted in June 2025.

Team
Canadian Valley Technology Center InvenTeam, El Reno, Oklahoma
Program
Lemelson-MIT InvenTeam; Microsoft #WhatsNext 2023 cohort
Funding
$7,500 Lemelson-MIT grant, plus $5,250 in sponsorships I secured
Patent
US 12,322,271 B2

Design process. Select a step to jump to it.

The problem

A student’s backpack carries what they need to get through the day, and forgetting one item can set back their schoolwork. Our team set out to build something that helps students keep track of those essentials.

How it works

  • A load cell in the base weighs the bag’s contents.
  • A microcontroller links to the user’s phone over Bluetooth, and an app manages the system.
  • Force-sensitive resistor pads in the straps detect when the bag is being worn.
  • A vibration motor alerts the user when an item is missing.

What I built and did

  • Built the strap electronics: force-sensitive resistors that sense when the bag is worn and a vibration motor that flags a missing item, prototyped on Arduino.
  • Helped develop a segmented base that spreads load across the strain gauges, so the system can tell individual items apart.
  • Kept the team’s engineering notebook and helped write the technical descriptions and engineering drawings for the patent.
  • Served as the team’s direct contact with the patent attorney through Microsoft’s #WhatsNext program, working with Doug Barker of Microsoft.
  • Secured $5,250 in corporate sponsorships on top of the Lemelson-MIT grant.
  • Presented at EurekaFest 2023 at MIT, answering technical questions on stage and talking with community members and prospective donors at our table.

MIT 2.007, Design and Manufacturing I

Bot-tholomew, a magnet-scoring robot

My personal robot for Design and Manufacturing I had to climb a steep curved track, then lift eight magnets 20 inches and place them all at once. I built the lift around a linkage that does the placing without an extra actuator.

Course
MIT 2.007, Design and Manufacturing I
Process
Sketch, cardboard prototype, CAD, physical build
Actuation
Two servos on separate channels; 1:3 gear train on the lift
Payload
8 magnets, raised 20 in

Design process. Select a step to jump to it.

Requirements

Climb
Drive up a curved track with a 36% grade at 1.25 ft/s
Score
Raise 8 magnets 20 in above the base of the track and place them simultaneously on the highest level of the scoring bin
Stability
Keep the center of gravity low for easy driving up and down the course

The lift

  • Parallel bars keep the magnets vertical through the whole drive and lift, swinging from about −45° to +45°.
  • Converts rotation into a smooth 20 in rise.
  • At full extension the arm moves 1.5 in forward and pushes the magnets onto the board, which removed the need for a fourth motor.
  • A 1:3 gear train gives the torque for the upward stroke.
  • Stowed, the magnet holder sits within the plate and wheels so the robot meets the width limit.

Annotated build

Canadian Valley Technology Center capstone

Period Pack, wearable heat therapy for cramps

For my capstone at Canadian Valley Technology Center, I designed a discreet belt bag that delivers medication-free heat relief for dysmenorrhea, with automatic safety cutoffs.

Program
Canadian Valley Technology Center capstone
My part
Electronic subsystem and CAD
Hardware
Arduino, heating-fabric resistor network, temperature sensor, insulation
Result
Held 42 °C contact temperature for 30 minutes

Design process. Select a step to jump to it.

Requirements

Discreet
Non-invasive and medication-free; wearable in class or on a walk without drawing attention
Heat
32–42 °C contact temperature for 30 minutes
Safety
Shuts off automatically if temperature or time exceeds safe limits

Electronics and testing

  • Designed the electronic subsystem: a heating-fabric resistor network driven by an Arduino, with a temperature sensor and a manual cutoff.
  • Held a 42 °C contact temperature for 30 minutes without climbing into an unsafe range.
  • Insulation kept heat where it belonged: a chocolate bar stored in the bag held up for 10 minutes while the pack heated on its low setting.
  • Both the manual and software cutoffs worked when the pack was left on too long or the temperature rose.
